content: Glipizide is an oral hypoglycemic medication that has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular mortality. It is important to discuss the potential risks, benefits, and alternative treatments with your doctor before starting this medication. Glipizide is prescribed to manage type 2 diabetes, a condition where the body does not use insulin effectively, leading to poor blood sugar control. It is particularly used in patients whose diabetes cannot be managed by diet alone. This medication works by stimulating the pancreas to release insulin and improving the body’s ability to use insulin efficiently. However, for glipizide to be effective, the pancreas must be capable of producing insulin. It is not suitable for treating type 1 diabetes, a condition where the body does not produce insulin at all. Glipizide may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Glipizide is available in tablet form and is typically taken once daily, 30 minutes before breakfast. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take the medication exactly as directed, without altering the dose or frequency. Continue taking glipizide even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Before starting glipizide, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to glipizide or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially antibiotics, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), dexamethasone, diuretics, estrogens, isoniazid, MAO inhibitors, medications for high blood pressure or heart disease, niacin, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, prednisone, probenecid, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney, liver, heart, or thyroid disease, or if you have a severe infection. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking glipizide, contact your doctor immediately. Additionally, if you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking glipizide. Avoid unnecessary or prolonged exposure to sunlight, and use protective clothing, sunglasses, and sunscreen, as glipizide may increase your skin’s sensitivity to sunlight. Follow all dietary and exercise recommendations provided by your doctor or dietitian. Maintaining a healthy diet is essential. Alcohol consumption may lower blood sugar levels, so consult your doctor about the safe use of alcoholic beverages while taking glipizide. If you forget to take a dose of glipizide, ask your doctor in advance what to do in such situations and write down their instructions for future reference. As a general rule, take the missed dose as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Glipizide may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), and know how to respond if these occur. Symptoms of hypoglycemia include shakiness, dizziness, sweating, nervousness, irritability, sudden mood changes, headache, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, hunger, and clumsy or jerky movements. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness. Ensure that family, friends, and others around you are aware of these symptoms and know to seek immediate medical attention if necessary. Symptoms of hyperglycemia include extreme thirst, frequent urination, extreme hunger, weakness, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can lead to a serious, life-threatening condition called diabetic ketoacidosis, which may present with symptoms such as dry mouth, upset stomach, vomiting, shortness of breath, fruity-smelling breath, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Glipizide may also cause other side effects. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience a skin rash, itching, redness, exaggerated sunburn, yellowing of the skin or eyes, light-colored stools, dark urine, unusual bleeding or bruising, fever, or sore throat. Serious side effects should be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store glipizide in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory, as they will monitor your response to glipizide through specific tests. Your doctor will also instruct you on how to monitor your blood or urine sugar levels at home. Always wear a diabetic identification bracelet to ensure proper treatment in emergencies. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
